raw_segments.text: In England, however, notwithstanding the flourishing state of its woolen manufacture, the price
of English wool has fallen very considerably since the time of Edward E.I.
There are many authentic records which demonstrate that, during the reign of that prince, towards
the middle of the 14th century, or about 1339, what was reckoned the moderate and reasonable
price of the tod, or twenty-eight pounds of English wool, was not less than ten shillings
of the money of those times, see Smith's Memoirs of Wool, Vol, IC567.
Also Vol, Roman II, containing, at the rate of twenty pence the ounce, six ounces of silver
tower weight, equal to about thirty shillings of our present money.
In the present times, one in twenty shillings the tod may be reckoned a good price for very
good English wool.
The money price of wool, therefore, in the time of Edward E.I., was to its money price
in the present times as ten to seven.
The superiority of its real price was still greater.
At the rate of six shillings and eight pence the quarter, ten shillings was in those ancient
times the price of twelve bushels of wheat.
At the rate of twenty-eight shillings the quarter, one in twenty shillings is in the
present times the price of six bushels only.
The proportion between the real price of ancient and modern times, therefore, is as twelve
to six, or as two to one.
In those ancient times, a tod of wool would have purchased twice the quantity of subsistence,
which it will purchase at present, and consequently twice the quantity of labor, if the real recompense
of labor had been the same in both periods.
